results.result: The authors developed synthspot, a simulation engine that generates silver standard synthetic spatial transcriptomics datasets with realistic tissue patterns featuring distinct regions and various abundance characteristics (uniform/diverse composition, distinct/overlapping regions, dominant/rare cell types). The simulator was validated to accurately model real data characteristics and produce comparable method performances between synthetic and real tissue patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C51-C64 collectively describe the development and validation of synthspot. The validation (C52-C53) is stated but references Appendix 1 for details. The description of the simulator's features is comprehensive and internally consistent, representing a methodological contribution that enables the benchmarking study.

results.result: The study benchmarked 11 deconvolution methods (8 spatial methods, 1 bulk method, 2 mapping methods) using 63 silver standards generated from 7 scRNA-seq datasets with 9 abundance patterns (10 replicates each), 3 gold standards from imaging data (seqFISH+ and STARMap), and 2 case studies (liver and melanoma). Methods were compared against two baselines (NNLS and Dirichlet null distribution), with consultation from original method authors to ensure appropriate parameter settings.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C36-C42, C65-C72 provide a comprehensive description of the benchmarking scope and methodology. The dataset composition is clearly specified with appropriate detail about data sources, replication strategy, and baseline comparisons. The consultation with method authors (C40) adds rigor to the evaluation.

results.result: Using three complementary metrics (RMSE for numerical accuracy, AUPR for presence/absence detection, JSD for distribution similarity), RCTD and cell2location were identified as the top two performers across all metrics in silver standards, followed by SpatialDWLS, stereoscope, and MuSiC. All other methods ranked worse than the NNLS baseline in at least one metric. Method performances were more consistent between abundance patterns than between datasets.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C81 describe the evaluation metrics and main performance findings. The use of three complementary metrics (C73-C76) is well-justified, and the ranking methodology using median values across replicates (C80) is appropriate. The findings are supported by references to Figures 2b and 3a (C77-C78), providing visual evidence for the rankings.

results.result: Most methods had worse performance in abundance patterns with a dominant cell type, with considerable variability between replicates due to different dominant cell types being selected. Only RCTD and cell2location consistently outperformed NNLS in all metrics for these challenging patterns. This pattern was also observed in gold standard FOVs dominated by one cell type, where half the methods did not perform well, with some methods (SPOTlight, DestVI, stereoscope, Tangram) predicting less variation in abundances.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84, C89-C93 describe consistent findings about method performance with dominant cell types across both silver and gold standards. The explanation for variability (C83) is logical, and the consistency between synthetic and real data (C90-C91) strengthens the validity of the simulation approach. References to figure supplements support these observations.

results.result: On gold standards (seqFISH+ and STARMap), cell2location, MuSiC, and RCTD were the top three performers and the only methods to outrank NNLS in all three metrics. Most methods performed worse on the STARMap dataset (996 genes) except for SpatialDWLS, SPOTlight, and Tangram. Rankings were based on average values across seven FOVs for seqFISH+ datasets.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88, C94 describe gold standard results with appropriate methodological details. The ranking approach for multi-FOV data (C87-C88) is clearly stated. The observation about STARMap performance (C94) is notable given its limited gene set, and the exception for marker-based methods is later explained in the discussion (C228-C229).

results.result: For rare cell type detection (5-15 times less abundant), RCTD and cell2location were the best performers. There is a strong correlation between cell type abundance and AUPR, with most methods detecting moderate/high abundance cell types but having lower sensitivity for rare cell types. The AUPR is substantially lower when the rare cell type is present in only one region versus across the entire tissue, indicating that prevalence is an important factor in detection.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C111 describe a focused analysis on rare cell type detection using 14 datasets. The rationale for using only AUPR (C102-C104) is well-justified based on the clinical importance of presence/absence over exact proportions. The findings about abundance-AUPR correlation (C106) and regional vs. global prevalence (C110-C111) are supported by Figure 4 and provide important insights into method limitations.

results.result: In stability analysis comparing intra-dataset (matched reference) versus inter-dataset (different platform reference) scenarios on brain cortex and cerebellum datasets, methods with better performance (cell2location, RCTD, SpatialDWLS, stereoscope) were generally more stable, with cell2location ranking first in all three datasets. Methods that accounted for platform effects in their models (cell2location, RCTD, stereoscope) showed better stability than those that did not (SpatialDWLS). Performance generally worsened in the inter-dataset scenario.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C125 describe a well-designed stability analysis using JSD to measure consistency between predictions with different references. The finding that methods accounting for technical variability are more stable (C118-C119) is logical and important for practical applications. The observation that SpatialDWLS performs well despite not modeling platform effects (C119) is an interesting exception. Results are supported by Figure 5.

results.result: In the liver case study with hepatocytes as a dominant cell type (>60% of tissue), RCTD and cell2location were top performers for both AUPR (detecting portal/central vein endothelial cells in their respective locations) and JSD (comparing to snRNA-seq ground truth), achieving JSD comparable to biological variation. Methods like Tangram, DSTG, and stereoscope had higher JSD than NNLS and predicted uniform distributions. Synthetic liver data with dominant cell type patterns showed strong correlation with real Visium data, validating the simulation approach.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C148 describe a comprehensive liver case study that validates findings from synthetic data. The use of biological knowledge about liver zonation (C132-C133) and snRNA-seq as ground truth (C135-C136) provides appropriate evaluation approaches. The validation using synthetic data (C146-C148) strengthens confidence in the benchmarking framework. Results are supported by Figure 6a and supplementary figures.

results.result: In the liver case study, there were inconsistencies between AUPR and JSD rankings, with Seurat and SpatialDWLS ranking highly for JSD but lowly for AUPR, because JSD is heavily influenced by the dominant cell type. Using combined references from three protocols did not necessarily yield best performance, and the best reference varied between methods. RCTD and Seurat showed highest stability across different references. When using the full atlas (23 vs 9 cell types), only RCTD, Seurat, SpatialDWLS, and MuSiC retained relative proportions of common cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C163 provide important insights about metric interpretation and reference dataset selection. The explanation for metric inconsistencies (C150-C152) is logical and demonstrates the importance of using complementary metrics (C153). The findings about reference dataset selection (C154-C160) and robustness to additional cell types (C161-C163) provide practical guidance. Results are supported by figure supplements.

results.result: In the melanoma case study using Molecular Cartography (MC) data as ground truth, cell2location, SPOTlight, and RCTD were the best performers with JSDs around 0.01. SPOTlight's good performance was an exception to its performance in silver standards. A qualitative analysis showed that higher-ranked methods exhibited the expected trend of endothelial cells being more abundant closer to blood vessels, while lower-ranked methods showed no correlation or noisy predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C183 describe the melanoma case study with appropriate methodological details about MC data processing (C169-C171) and evaluation approaches (C174). The qualitative validation using biological knowledge about endothelial cell localization (C178-C183) provides additional confidence in the rankings. The exception for SPOTlight (C176) is noted. Results are supported by Figure 6b-c and supplementary figures.

results.result: Most methods deconvolved silver standard datasets in less than 30 minutes with slight runtime variability. Model-based methods (DestVI, stereoscope, cell2location, STRIDE) can reuse models across datasets from the same reference, reducing runtime, but are computationally intensive and benefit from GPU acceleration. In scalability testing (16 combinations of spots and genes), Tangram, Seurat, and SPOTlight had constant runtime across dimensions, deconvolving the largest dataset in under 10 minutes. Stereoscope was least scalable, taking over 8 hours for the largest dataset. Methods using only marker genes (RCTD, SpatialDWLS, Tangram, SPOTlight) showed better scalability.
results.evaluation: Claims C184-C203 provide comprehensive runtime and scalability analysis. The experimental design (C191-C194) is appropriate, testing realistic dataset dimensions. The findings about model reuse (C186-C187), GPU requirements (C188-C190), and marker gene methods (C199) provide practical insights. The note about parameter flexibility (C201-C203) acknowledges that runtime can be optimized. Results are supported by Figure 7.

results.result: Overall findings indicate that RCTD, cell2location, and SpatialDWLS were the highest ranked methods, consistent with previous studies. However, over half of the methods did not outperform the baseline (NNLS) and bulk deconvolution method (MuSiC). Results were consistent across silver standards, gold standards, and case studies, demonstrating generalizability of the benchmarking framework. The abundance pattern and reference dataset had the most significant impact on performance, with even top methods struggling with challenging patterns (rare cell types in one region, highly dominant cell types). Methods accounting for technical variability (cell2location, RCTD) were more stable than those that did not (SpatialDWLS).
results.evaluation: Claims C210-C218 summarize the main findings with appropriate citations to previous work (C211). The surprising finding that many methods don't outperform simple baselines (C212) is important. The consistency across datasets (C213-C214) validates the approach. The identification of key factors affecting performance (C215-C218) provides actionable insights for method users and developers.

results.result: The number of genes per cell type (correlated with sequencing depth) significantly impacts deconvolution performance. Methods were less accurate in datasets with fewer genes per cell type. The kidney dataset (most cell types <1000 genes) was most challenging with RMSE and JSD closer to null distribution, while the brain cortex dataset (3000-9000 genes per cell type) showed much better performance despite having more cell types. This trend was also observed in the STARMap gold standard (996 genes), though marker-based methods (SpatialDWLS, SPOTlight, Tangram) were less affected.
results.evaluation: Claims C219-C229 identify an important factor affecting method performance that is supported by comparisons across multiple datasets (C220-C227). The explanation for why marker-based methods are less affected (C228-C229) is logical, though presented as speculation. The findings are supported by references to figure supplements and provide practical guidance about reference dataset quality requirements.

results.result: The authors recommend RCTD as a good starting point due to being one of the best and fastest methods with CPU parallelization capability. As a general guideline, they recommend comparing results from multiple methods, especially cell2location and RCTD, with highly contradictory predictions indicating poor reference quality. They recommend obtaining matched scRNA-seq and spatial data from the same sample to reduce biological variability, or using a reference with sufficient sequencing depth (>1000 genes per cell type) from a single platform. Synthspot can be used to evaluate reference quality, with high-quality references enabling cell2location and RCTD to achieve AUPR close to 1 and JSD close to 0.
results.evaluation: Claims C233-C244 provide practical recommendations based on the benchmarking results. The recommendation of RCTD (C233-C235) is justified by the performance and scalability results. The guidelines for reference dataset selection (C238-C241) are based on the stability and gene number findings. The suggestion to use synthspot for quality evaluation (C242-C244) provides a practical tool for users. These are reasonable inferences from the results.

results.result: The benchmarking pipeline is completely reproducible and accessible through Nextflow at github.com/saeyslab/spotless-benchmark, with each method implemented in Docker containers enabling use without prior installation. The pipeline seamlessly integrates synthetic data generation, deconvolution, and performance evaluation, providing a reliable and reproducible evaluation framework for current and upcoming deconvolution tools.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44, C245, C247-C248 describe the computational infrastructure and its value. The use of Nextflow and Docker containers (C43-C44) ensures reproducibility and ease of use. The integration of the complete workflow (C245) is a significant contribution. The claims about providing a valuable resource (C247-C248) are reasonable given the comprehensive nature of the benchmark.

results.result: Background claims establish that spatial transcriptomics technologies profile transcriptomes while preserving spatial context, which is essential for studying cell-cell interactions and tissue architecture. ST approaches are categorized into imaging-based (subcellular resolution, high sensitivity, limited genes) and sequencing-based (transcriptome-wide, initially 100 µm spots, now approaching subcellular resolution) methods. Since spots don't necessarily correspond to individual cells, computational deconvolution methods are necessary, which use reference scRNA-seq data to infer cell type proportions (deconvolution) or probabilities (mapping) per spot.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C13-C31 provide background knowledge about spatial transcriptomics and deconvolution methods, supported by appropriate citations (Wagner et al. 2016, Asp et al. 2020, Eng et al. 2019, Xia et al. 2019, Rodriques et al. 2019, Ståhl et al. 2016, Chen et al. 2022, Cho et al. 2021, Longo et al. 2021). These establish the context and motivation for the benchmarking study.

results.result: Previous benchmarking studies exist but have not evaluated the added value of spatial-specific algorithms compared to baselines, have not assessed which algorithms handle challenging scenarios (highly abundant or rare cell types), and have not assessed stability to variations in reference datasets from different technologies or protocols.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 identify gaps in previous benchmarking work (citing Li et al. 2022, Yan and Sun 2023, Li et al. 2023b) that motivate the current study. These are reasonable assessments of the literature that justify the study's focus areas.

results.result: Existing synthetic datasets and simulators have limitations for deconvolution benchmarking: synthetic datasets typically have random compositions not reflecting tissue regions with distinct compositions; general-purpose simulators focus on other tasks and are unsuitable for deconvolution; generative/kinetic models (scDesign3, scMultiSim) are computationally intensive and cannot model entire transcriptomes; SRTSim focuses on gene expression trends without explicit tissue composition modeling; spaSim models only tissue composition without gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C50 identify limitations of existing approaches with appropriate citations (Song and Wang 2024, Li et al. 2023a, Zhu 2023, Feng et al. 2023), providing justification for developing synthspot. These are reasonable assessments of existing tools' capabilities and limitations.

results.result: Lowly abundant cell types (stem cells, progenitor cells, circulating tumor cells) play important roles in development or disease progression, and their occurrence is used to create prognostic models of patient outcomes, making accurate detection of rare cell types a key aspect of deconvolution tools.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 provide biological context for the importance of rare cell type detection, supported by citations (Jindal et al. 2018, Ali et al. 2016, Sato et al. 2005). This justifies the focused analysis on rare cell type detection.

results.result: The choice of reference dataset has been shown to have the largest impact on bulk deconvolution predictions, and deconvolution methods should ideally account for platform effects (capture biases from differing protocols and technologies used to generate scRNA-seq and ST data).
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C113 provide context for the stability analysis, with C112 supported by citation to Vallania et al. 2018. C113 is a reasonable inference about what methods should do given the importance of reference dataset choice.

results.result: Melanoma poses a significant challenge in therapeutic and research efforts due to its high degree of heterogeneity and plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claim C164 provides biological context for the melanoma case study. This is stated as established knowledge about melanoma and provides justification for using it as a challenging test case.

results.result: The study performed a thorough investigation of biologically relevant aspects of deconvolution, evaluating 11 methods on 63 silver standards, 3 gold standards, and 2 Visium datasets using three complementary metrics, with two baselines (NNLS and Dirichlet null distribution) for every analysis. The case studies demonstrated two approaches for evaluating methods without absolute ground truth: using proportions from another technology as proxy, and leveraging existing spot annotations (zonation, blood vessel annotations).
results.evaluation: Claims C204-C209 summarize the study's scope and methodological contributions. These are accurate summaries of the work described in detail elsewhere in the manuscript.

results.result: Runtime and scalability are factors to consider in addition to performance. GPU acceleration was used for Tangram, DestVI, stereoscope, and cell2location in this study, and users without GPU access might need to train on fewer epochs or select a subset of genes when using these methods on CPU.
results.evaluation: Claims C230-C232 provide practical context about computational requirements. C231 describes the study's computational setup, and C232 offers reasonable recommendations for users with different computational resources.

results.result: As spatial omics is an emerging field, the development of new deconvolution methods can be anticipated in the future.
results.evaluation: Claim C246 is a reasonable speculation about future developments in the field that provides context for the ongoing value of the benchmarking framework.

results.result: The study developed a comprehensive benchmarking framework including the synthspot simulator to generate 63 silver standards and 3 gold standards, evaluating 11 deconvolution methods (8 spatial, 1 bulk, 2 mapping) plus two baselines (NNLS and null distribution) using three complementary metrics (RMSE, AUPR, JSD). The framework is fully reproducible via a Nextflow pipeline with Docker containers.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly praise the methodological rigor and reproducibility framework. Reviewer 1 states the study 'provides a reliable and reproducible evaluation framework' and notes 'a full Nextflow pipeline' and 'methods implemented in Docker containers' as strengths. Reviewer 2 highlights '(i) a full Nextflow pipeline to reproduce their analyses; (ii) methods implemented in Docker containers; (iii) a fairly decent assessment of their simulator' as elements 'above the average for a benchmarking study.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'they present a reusable and extendable platform' and notes 'the reproducibility of the methods described will have significant utility.'

results.result: RCTD and cell2location are the top-performing methods across silver and gold standards, with SpatialDWLS also ranking highly. Surprisingly, over half of the dedicated spatial deconvolution methods did not outperform the simple NNLS baseline, with only RCTD and cell2location consistently outperforming NNLS in challenging scenarios like dominant cell type patterns.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. Reviewer 1 states 'The authors demonstrate the strengths of RCTD, cell2location, and SpatialDWLS for their performance, while also revealing the limitations of many methods when compared to simpler baselines.' Reviewer 2 notes 'surprisingly, several methods performed below this baseline.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'RCTD, SpatialDWLS and Cell2location typically provide the best results' and acknowledges 'many methods are still outperformed by bulk deconvolution methods (e.g. Music or NNLS).' The consistency of findings is noted as 'very similar conclusions to other deconvolution benchmarking paper' by Reviewer 3.

results.result: All methods showed significantly decreased performance in challenging abundance patterns, particularly with highly abundant/dominant cell types and rare cell types. RCTD and cell2location were best at detecting rare cell types, but even top-performing methods struggled when rare cell types were present in only one region. There is a strong correlation between cell type abundance and detection performance (AUPR).
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these findings without challenge. Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'the results from their thorough analysis support the conclusions that creating cell type deconvolution algorithms that can handle both cell abundance and rarity throughout a given tissue sample are challenging.' The reviewers do not question the observation that performance decreases with extreme abundance patterns, and Reviewer 1 notes the study addresses 'biologically relevant, previously unconsidered aspects' including these challenging scenarios.

results.result: Different reference datasets can result in substantially different predicted proportions. Methods accounting for technical variability (cell2location, RCTD) showed greater stability to reference dataset changes than those that did not (e.g., SpatialDWLS). Cell2location ranked first in stability across all three tested datasets, while NNLS and MuSiC were consistently in the bottom three.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledges this finding, stating 'The authors make a point to address both inter- and intra- dataset reference handling, which has a significant impact on performance' and notes 'supplying optimal reference data is - potentially most - important to achieve the best performance.' Reviewer 3 also observes that 'bulk' methods like MuSiC and NNLS 'are also among the most sensitive when using an external (inter) dataset,' which aligns with the stability findings. No reviewer challenges these stability results.

results.result: In the liver case study with a dominant hepatocyte cell type (>60% of tissue), RCTD and cell2location were top performers achieving JSD comparable to biological variation. Methods like Tangram, DSTG, SPOTlight, and stereoscope performed worse than NNLS, with some predicting uniform distributions. The study demonstrated that using combined reference datasets did not necessarily yield best performance, and complementary metrics (AUPR and JSD) must both be considered.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the liver case study findings. Reviewer 1 notes the study includes 'case studies on liver and melanoma tissues' as part of the comprehensive evaluation. Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'the authors thoroughly and rigorously compare methods while addressing situational discrepancies in model performance, indicative of a strong analysis.' The liver results are presented as validation of the silver standard findings, and no reviewer questions this validation approach or the specific performance rankings.

results.result: In the melanoma case study, cell2location, SPOTlight, and RCTD were the best performers with JSDs around 0.01. SPOTlight performed exceptionally well in this dataset (an exception to its silver standard performance). A qualitative analysis showed that higher-ranked methods better captured the expected trend of endothelial cells being more abundant closer to blood vessels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the melanoma case study without challenge. Reviewer 1 mentions 'case studies on liver and melanoma tissues' as part of the evaluation scope. Reviewer 3 notes 'the authors achieve their aim to benchmark different deconvolution methods' and acknowledges the thoroughness of the analysis. The qualitative validation approach using blood vessel annotations is consistent with Reviewer 3's observation that the study demonstrates 'two approaches for evaluating deconvolution methods in datasets lacking an absolute ground truth.'

results.result: Most methods deconvolve silver standard datasets in less than 30 minutes with slight runtime variability. Tangram, Seurat, and SPOTlight showed constant runtime across all dimensions and processed the largest dataset in under 10 minutes. Stereoscope was the least scalable, taking over 8 hours for the largest dataset. Model-based methods (DestVI, stereoscope, cell2location, STRIDE) benefit from model reuse but require GPU acceleration.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledges the importance of these findings, stating 'it's important to realize that deconvolution approaches are typically part of larger exploratory data analysis (EDA) efforts and require users to change parameters and input data multiple times. Thus, running time, computing needs, and scalability are probably key factors that researchers would like to consider when looking to deconvolve their datasets.' No reviewer challenges the runtime or scalability measurements, and the practical importance is affirmed.

results.result: The number of genes per cell type (correlated with sequencing depth) has a significant impact on deconvolution performance. Methods were less accurate in datasets with fewer genes per cell type (e.g., kidney dataset with <1000 genes per cell type was most challenging). The brain cortex dataset with 3000-9000 features per cell type led to much better performance despite having more cell types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these observations about the impact of gene number on performance. Reviewer 3 notes 'supplying optimal reference data is - potentially most - important to achieve the best performance,' which aligns with the finding that reference quality (including gene depth) matters significantly. The observation is presented as an analysis finding without reviewer objection.

results.result: Results were consistent across silver standards, gold standards, and case studies (liver and melanoma), demonstrating the generalizability and applicability of the simulation and benchmarking framework.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'A key aspect of their results is that they are generally very concordant between real and synthetic datasets.' Reviewer 3 notes the study 'reach very similar conclusions to other deconvolution benchmarking paper' and that 'the authors achieve their aim to benchmark different deconvolution methods.' The consistency across different evaluation approaches is affirmed by reviewers as a strength of the study.

results.result: The study recommends RCTD as a good starting point due to being one of the best and fastest methods with CPU parallelization support. General guidelines include comparing multiple methods (especially cell2location and RCTD), obtaining matched scRNA-seq and spatial data from the same sample, using reference datasets with sufficient sequencing depth (>1000 genes per cell type), and using synthspot to evaluate reference quality.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these recommendations. Reviewer 1 notes the study 'provides a resource for those seeking to improve or develop new deconvolution methods,' implicitly supporting the practical guidance. Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'experimental design or sample matching is at least equally important to selecting the ideal deconvolution tool,' which aligns with the recommendation to obtain matched samples. The recommendations follow logically from the benchmarking results that reviewers have accepted.

results.result: Existing synthetic datasets and simulators have limitations: synthetic datasets typically have random spot compositions that don't reflect tissue regions with distinct compositions; general-purpose simulators focus on other tasks and are unsuitable for deconvolution; specific simulators like scDesign3 and scMultiSim are computationally intensive and cannot model entire transcriptomes; SRTSim doesn't explicitly model tissue composition while spaSim doesn't model gene expression.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes the study provides 'a fairly decent assessment of their simulator compared to other spatial omics simulators,' implicitly accepting the characterization of existing simulator limitations. Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'Major strengths of the simulation engine include the ability to downsample and recapitulate several cell and tissue organization patterns,' which contrasts with the limitations of other simulators. No reviewer challenges the stated limitations of existing approaches.

results.result: The case studies demonstrated two approaches for evaluating deconvolution methods without absolute ground truth: (1) using proportions from another sequencing/spatial technology as a proxy, and (2) leveraging existing spot annotations (e.g., zonation, blood vessel annotations).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these methodological contributions without challenge. Reviewer 1 notes the study addresses 'biologically relevant, previously unconsidered aspects.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'the authors thoroughly and rigorously compare methods' and that the study demonstrates practical evaluation approaches. The validation strategies are consistent with the reviewers' recognition of the study's thoroughness.

results.result: As spatial omics is an emerging field, new deconvolution methods can be anticipated. The benchmark provides a reliable and reproducible evaluation framework for current and upcoming tools, making it a valuable resource for researchers.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states the study 'provides a resource for those seeking to improve or develop new deconvolution methods' and 'has the potential to also set the standard of benchmarks higher.' Reviewer 2 notes 'The Nextflow pipeline will make the prospect of including new reference datasets and new computational methods easier,' acknowledging the framework's utility for future methods. Reviewer 3 confirms 'the reproducibility of the methods described will have significant utility for researchers looking to develop cell type deconvolution algorithms.'
